title: How to Retire at 60 With a Plan for the Gap Years
metaDescription: Learn how to retire at 60 by calculating your spending needs, covering health insurance before Medicare, and funding the years before Social Security.
h1: How to Retire at 60 With a Plan for the Gap Years
cardBlurb: A spending-based way to test retirement at 60, including the health coverage gap and the years before Social Security.
introText:
You can retire at 60 if your savings can cover your spending, health insurance until Medicare, and the years before Social Security begins. The first step is to estimate what you would spend each year, then separate the costs you must pay at 60 from the costs you expect after benefits begin.

At 60, you are past the usual early-withdrawal penalty age for a 401(k) or individual retirement account (IRA). You are also about five years from Medicare eligibility, and you cannot yet claim Social Security retirement benefits. Those dates make a single retirement savings number less useful than a plan for each stretch of time.

sections.heading: A Spending-Based Savings Calculation
sections.body:
Your spending estimate is the starting point for deciding whether retirement at 60 is affordable. Write down a year of expected retirement costs, including housing, food, transportation, taxes, and health coverage. Use the bills you can identify rather than a percentage of your current pay. If a cost will change when work ends, make a separate estimate for the retirement version.

For a rough calculation, multiply annual spending by 25. That is the arithmetic behind a 4% first-year withdrawal: $1 divided by 25 is four cents. A hypothetical $60,000 annual budget therefore points to $1.5 million before accounting for future guaranteed income. The 4% rule is a starting point, not a promise that a balance will last. At 60, you may need the money for more than 30 years.

Guaranteed income can reduce the amount your portfolio must eventually provide. Suppose your hypothetical $60,000 budget includes an expected $20,000 a year in Social Security beginning at 67. From 67 onward, the remaining $40,000 a year suggests $1 million at a 4% rate. That subtraction does not pay the bills from 60 through 66. Make a separate bridge-year calculation for those years, when the full spending amount must come from other sources. Keep health coverage costs in the years when you expect to pay them.

sections.heading: Health Insurance Before Medicare
sections.body:
Retiring at 60 generally leaves about five years before [Medicare eligibility](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/get-more-coverage/when-does-medicare-coverage-start) begins at 65. Price coverage for that entire gap before setting a retirement date. Employer coverage under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA), a marketplace plan, and a spouse's plan are possible routes. Which route you can use, and what it costs you, belongs in your own retirement budget.

Start by asking what coverage will be available on the date your job ends. If a spouse's plan is a possibility, confirm when you could join it and what the added premium would be. If you are considering COBRA or a marketplace plan, get figures for the coverage you would choose. Put premiums and the amount you expect to pay when you receive care into separate budget lines. A low premium alone will not tell you what a year of coverage might cost.

Then check the transition at 65 rather than treating it as the end of healthcare spending. Your budget still needs a health coverage line after Medicare begins. If the five-year gap makes your projected withdrawals too high, moving the retirement date closer to 65 or working part time may reduce the amount you need to draw from savings.

sections.heading: Social Security Timing and the Bridge Years
sections.body:
Social Security retirement benefits cannot start at 60. The earliest claiming age is 62, so a plan to stop working at 60 needs another source of income for at least the first two years. The [Social Security Administration's early-claiming rules](https://www.ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/agereduction.html) also show that claiming before full retirement age permanently reduces the monthly benefit. Do not use a later-age benefit estimate to fill a budget gap that begins at 62.

You can also plan to claim after full retirement age. The Social Security Administration explains that [delaying benefits up to age 70](https://www.ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/delayret.html) increases the monthly amount. A later claim means drawing on savings or earning income for longer, so compare the higher benefit with the extra bridge years it requires.

Build one annual income line for each year from 60 through your intended claiming age. Enter zero for Social Security before that age. Then enter the benefit estimate for the age you chose, rather than applying one amount across the whole plan. Try an earlier and a later claim using a [Social Security retirement calculator](/calculators/social-security-retirement-calculator/). The question is whether you can fund the waiting years without leaving too little invested for the years that follow.

sections.heading: Withdrawal Order and Taxes
sections.body:
At 60, withdrawals from a 401(k) or IRA generally no longer face the 10% additional tax that applies to withdrawals before age 59½. Traditional 401(k) and IRA withdrawals can still produce ordinary income tax. Roth IRA earnings have a separate five-year rule to consider. Account access and after-tax spending are therefore different numbers: an account withdrawal may need to exceed the amount you intend to spend.

Cash and taxable accounts can fund some bridge-year costs, while tax-deferred withdrawals can supply the rest. There is no single account order that suits every person. Write down how much you plan to take from each account in each year, then estimate the tax on that mix. If the tax estimate increases the withdrawal you need, put the larger withdrawal back into your savings calculation.

Pay particular attention to the year Social Security begins. Income that was funded entirely from savings may then come from both savings and benefits, changing the withdrawal amount you need. Social Security benefits may also affect your tax calculation; [whether Social Security is taxable](/guides/is-social-security-taxable/) explains that question in more detail. Keep enough accessible money for the first bridge year so the plan does not depend on selling investments on a particular date.

sections.heading: Part-Time Work as a Bridge
sections.body:
Part-time work can lower the amount you need to withdraw between 60 and your Social Security claiming age. Treat it as a specific income estimate rather than a vague fallback. Write down the hours you would be willing to work, the pay you could reasonably expect, and the year you would stop. Then run the retirement calculation once with that income and once without it.

For example, if a hypothetical plan calls for $60,000 of spending and $15,000 of part-time income at 60, savings must provide the remaining $45,000 before taxes. If the work ends at 63 and Social Security starts later, the savings requirement rises again for the intervening years. A year-by-year budget shows that change; a single average income figure hides it.

Phased retirement may also give you more time to settle the health insurance question. Before relying on continued employment for coverage, confirm whether the proposed hours come with a plan you can use. If the work or coverage is uncertain, base your retirement decision on the version without them. Someone who does not want to work after 60 should fund the bridge entirely from savings or consider a later retirement date.

sections.heading: Risks in a Longer Retirement
sections.body:
A retirement beginning at 60 may last more than 30 years, so the 4% calculation needs a stress test. Try the same spending plan with a lower withdrawal rate and see whether your savings still cover it. Also test a higher health coverage cost for ages 60 through 64. These are planning scenarios, not predictions, but they show which assumption your retirement date depends on.

A weak investment period early in retirement creates another risk: you may have to sell more of your portfolio to raise the same spending amount. Identify expenses you could reduce for a year if withdrawals need to come down. Keep that reduced budget specific. Cutting a planned trip is different from assuming you can cut housing or health coverage at short notice.

Check how much of the plan depends on one future event. A part-time job may not materialize, or you may decide to claim Social Security at a different age. Recalculate without the income you are least certain about. If retirement at 60 works only when every estimate goes your way, working longer or lowering planned spending gives the budget more room. For a longer comparison, [retiring at 40](/guides/how-to-retire-at-40/) requires an even longer funding period, while [retiring at 67](/guides/how-to-retire-at-67/) shortens the years before Medicare and Social Security.

sections.heading: A First-Week Retirement Checklist
sections.body:
The first task is to build a year-by-year budget from age 60 through your planned Social Security claiming age. Begin with annual spending. Add a separate health coverage estimate for the years before 65, and mark when any part-time pay would begin and end. Keep Social Security at zero until the year you plan to claim it. This gives you the annual amount your savings would need to provide.

Next, list your available cash, taxable savings, 401(k) balances, and IRA balances. Assign a possible withdrawal source to each bridge year and include estimated taxes. Compare those withdrawals with your balances rather than assuming the 25-times-spending calculation covers every year. At your intended claiming age, calculate the spending left after Social Security and use that amount for a separate long-term withdrawal check.

Finally, run a less comfortable version of the plan: higher health costs, no part-time income, or a lower withdrawal rate. Choose a retirement date only after you can see which of those changes the budget can absorb. If the gap years remain unaffordable, the next decision is concrete: reduce spending, earn income during the gap, or retire later. Put your expected spending and benefit ages on one page today to work out how to retire at 60.

faqs.question: How much money do I need to retire at 60?
faqs.answer: Start with your expected annual spending and multiply it by 25 for a rough estimate based on a 4% withdrawal rate. Then account for guaranteed income when it begins and calculate the earlier bridge years separately. Add the health coverage and tax costs that apply to your plan. The result is a planning estimate, not a guaranteed savings target.

faqs.question: Can I collect Social Security when I retire at 60?
faqs.answer: No. Social Security retirement benefits can begin as early as 62, so you need another way to fund at least the first two years. Claiming before full retirement age permanently reduces the monthly benefit; delaying past full retirement age up to 70 increases it.

faqs.question: How do I get health insurance if I retire at 60?
faqs.answer: Plan for roughly five years before Medicare eligibility generally begins at 65. Possible coverage includes employer COBRA, a marketplace plan, or a spouse's plan. Confirm which coverage you can use and enter its expected costs into each year of your retirement budget.

faqs.question: Can I withdraw from my 401(k) or IRA at 60 without a penalty?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. At 60, you are past age 59½, so the usual 10% additional tax on early 401(k) and IRA withdrawals no longer applies. Traditional account withdrawals can still be subject to ordinary income tax, and Roth IRA earnings also need to meet the five-year rule.

faqs.question: Should I work part time after retiring at 60?
faqs.answer: Part-time work can reduce withdrawals during the years before Social Security begins, if you are willing and able to do it. Calculate the plan both with and without that pay. If retirement at 60 works only with uncertain part-time income, consider more savings, lower spending, or a later retirement date.
